scenes.title: Eigenvalues as invariant directions
scenes.objective: Understand Av=λv and the determinant condition.

ask.q: For A=diag(2,3), what are its eigenvalues?
ask.nudge: A diagonal matrix already displays its invariant coordinate directions.

body: A matrix transforms vectors. An eigenvector is a non-zero vector whose direction is unchanged by the transformation: Av=λv. The scalar λ is its eigenvalue.
Rearranging gives (A−λI)v=0. A non-zero solution exists exactly when A−λI is singular, hence det(A−λI)=0.
The zero vector is excluded because it satisfies the equation for every λ and carries no directional information.

scenes.title: Characteristic polynomial and 2×2 shortcut
scenes.objective: Compute eigenvalues and check them with trace and determinant.

blocks.body: p_A(λ)=det(λI−A). Its roots are the eigenvalues, counted with algebraic multiplicity.
p_A(λ)=λ²−tr(A)λ+det(A). Thus the sum of roots is tr(A), and their product is det(A).

ask.q: A 2×2 matrix has trace 7 and determinant 12. What are its eigenvalues if real?
ask.nudge: Find two numbers with sum 7 and product 12.

scenes.title: Find the eigenvectors
scenes.objective: Solve the homogeneous system for each eigenvalue.
scenes.problem: Take A=[[2,1],[1,2]]. Its eigenvalues are 1 and 3.

scenario.teaser: Two directions scale by different factors.
scenario.title: A diagonal transformation in two dimensions
body: For A=diag(2,3), the coordinate axes are invariant directions.
The first component doubles and the second triples. These scale factors are the eigenvalues.
The same idea extends to non-diagonal matrices after changing to an eigenvector basis.

scenes.title: Diagonalisation and multiplicities
scenes.objective: Decide whether a matrix has enough independent eigenvectors.

blocks.body: Algebraic multiplicity (AM) is the root multiplicity in p_A. Geometric multiplicity (GM) is dim null(A−λI). Always 1≤GM≤AM.
An n×n matrix is diagonalisable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Distinct eigenvalues guarantee this; repeated eigenvalues require checking eigenspace dimensions.
A=[[1,1],[0,1]] has characteristic polynomial (λ−1)² but null(A−I) has dimension 1. It has only one independent eigenvector and is not diagonalisable.

ask.q: A 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues 2 (AM 2, GM 1) and 5 (AM 1, GM 1). Is it diagonalisable?
ask.nudge: Add the dimensions of the eigenspaces.

blocks.body: Every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Hence A=QDQᵀ, with QᵀQ=I.
A general diagonalisation uses P⁻¹. For a real symmetric matrix, P can be chosen orthogonal, so P⁻¹=Pᵀ. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

ask.q: Does a real symmetric matrix necessarily have positive eigenvalues?

scenes.title: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
scenes.objective: Substitute a matrix into its characteristic polynomial.

blocks.body: For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], p_A(λ)=λ²−4λ+3. Thus A²−4A+3I=0. Indeed A²=[[5,4],[4,5]], and the expression is the zero matrix.
Cayley–Hamilton reduces higher powers to lower powers. When det(A)≠0, it can also express A⁻¹ as a polynomial in A.

ask.q: If p_A(λ)=λ²−5λ+6, write the matrix identity.
ask.nudge: Replace λ by A and the constant 6 by 6I.

scenes.title: Powers and exam checks
scenes.objective: Choose the fastest route for common matrix questions.

blocks.body: If A=PDP⁻¹, then Aᵏ=PDᵏP⁻¹. Raise each diagonal entry of D to the kth power.
A is invertible iff zero is not an eigenvalue iff det(A)≠0. The determinant is the product of eigenvalues, with multiplicity.

ask.q: If eigenvalues of A are 2 and −1, what are the eigenvalues of A⁴?
ask.nudge: Raise each eigenvalue to the fourth power.

scenes.title: Why diagonalisation matters in a statistical model
body: Consider a population transition or an iterative numerical update x_(t+1)=Ax_t. An eigenvector is a direction that the update does not rotate; it only scales it by λ.
If |λ|<1, repeated updates shrink that component. If |λ|>1, it grows. If λ is negative, its sign alternates. This is why eigenvalues appear in stability and long-run behaviour.

ask.q: If every eigenvalue of a diagonalisable matrix has modulus less than one, what happens to A^k as k grows?
ask.nudge: Each diagonal entry in D^k tends to zero.

scenario.teaser: A repeated update is applied to a vector of rates.
scenario.title: Eigenvalues and stability of an iterative update
body: A system updates a two-component state by x_(t+1)=Ax_t. If A is diagonalisable, A^k=P D^k P^-1.
The long-run behaviour is controlled by powers of the eigenvalues. Components with modulus below one decay; components above one grow.
This interpretation is useful in Markov-chain convergence, numerical iteration and dynamic models, while the exact stochastic interpretation depends on the model assumptions.

scenes.title: Worked decision: a repeated eigenvalue
scenes.objective: Show why a repeated root needs an eigenspace check.

ask.q: For B=[[1,1],[0,1]], what is the dimension of null(B−I)?

steps.why: The only eigenvalue is 1 with algebraic multiplicity 2.
The eigenspace is span{(1,0)}, of dimension 1.
Only one independent eigenvector exists, so B is not diagonalisable.

scenes.title: Trap check: six claims
scenes.objective: Separate always-true theorems from common overclaims.
scenes.intro: Judge each statement before revealing the explanation.

items.claim: The zero vector is an eigenvector.
Distinct eigenvalues have linearly independent eigenvectors.
items.why: This theorem guarantees diagonalisation when there are n distinct eigenvalues.

items.claim: A repeated eigenvalue means the matrix is not diagonalisable.
items.why: A repeated eigenvalue can have geometric multiplicity equal to algebraic multiplicity.

items.claim: Geometric multiplicity is at most algebraic multiplicity.
Every real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable.
The constant term in p_A(A) is a scalar times the identity.
items.why: A scalar matrix term is cI, not c alone.

scenes.title: The complete decision sequence
scenes.objective: Leave with a reliable exam method.
body: 1. Form det(λI−A)=0 and solve for eigenvalues.
2. Check roots using their sum (trace) and product (determinant).
3. For each λ, solve (A−λI)v=0 and find the eigenspace dimension.
4. Add geometric multiplicities: n independent eigenvectors means diagonalisation.
5. If A is real symmetric, use orthogonal diagonalisation immediately.
6. For powers and inverses, consider A=PDP⁻¹ or substitute A into Cayley–Hamilton.
